current_episode.title: Ep.182 -Building a Reputation Management Business In Full Flight

guest.bio_context: Shane Barker is a C-level strategist and tech entrepreneur who has spent over two decades building, scaling, and productizing businesses. He is a member of the Forbes Coaches Council and a regular contributor to Forbes, HuffPost, and Inc. He has taught personal branding and influencer marketing at UCLA and hosted the Marketing Growth Podcast, where he interviewed leaders from companies like Moz and Socialnomics. Earlier in his career, he owned a bar in Chico, California and ran a real estate company that helped clients go from zero to $25 million.

context.real_quote: We were the first company to ever remove reviews on Amazon. Now we work with 700 brands and removed over 16,000 reviews. But we didn't start off with tons of customers — we paved the way.

pending_qa.q: How long did it take Tracefuse to validate and crack its core Amazon review removal process?
pending_qa.r: Shane Barker states it took Tracefuse two full years to crack the code on their review removal process, during which they were burning through capital with no guaranteed outcome. He admits that had he known upfront it would take two years, he might have reconsidered launching the business.

pending_qa.q: How did Shane Barker validate the market demand for Tracefuse before building the product?
pending_qa.r: Barker validated demand by asking existing clients at Shane Barker Consulting about their biggest pain points, and reviews consistently came up as a critical issue for Amazon sellers. He then paid Amazon experts at their hourly rates to consult on feasibility, asking targeted questions about whether review removal was possible and what obstacles had been encountered historically.

pending_qa.q: How did Tracefuse use AI to scale its review monitoring operations?
pending_qa.r: In the early days, Tracefuse relied entirely on human reviewers to manually scan hundreds of reviews daily for Amazon guideline violations, which was difficult to scale. More than three years ago, before tools like Gemini and Claude became mainstream, Tracefuse integrated AI to automate the initial flagging process, reducing the number of reviews a human needed to manually check — cutting the workload from around 1,000 reviews down to roughly 400 per person.

pending_qa.q: Who were the first hires at Tracefuse and what roles did they fill?
pending_qa.r: The first hire was Susan, a trusted team member already working across Shane Barker's other businesses, who was brought on to help with operations, case filing, and fact-finding during the validation phase. The second hire was a dedicated 'filer' — someone trained to file review removal cases with Amazon — since a formal sales team was not yet needed while the company was still in validation mode.

pending_qa.q: What mindset does Shane Barker recommend for Amazon sellers regarding platform dependency?
pending_qa.r: Barker argues that Amazon sellers must internalize that they are 'renting Amazon space' — the platform does not owe them anything and will make decisions based on its own business interests, not individual sellers'. He draws a parallel to Instagram, Facebook, and X, urging sellers to focus on how they can adapt and move with platform changes rather than expecting the platform to protect their business.

pending_qa.q: How did Tracefuse's review removal methodology change over its first five and a half years?
pending_qa.r: Barker states that if you compared Tracefuse's filing methods from five and a half years ago to today, they are 'almost polar opposites,' largely because Amazon frequently restructures its internal departments, changes filing processes, and reassigns leadership. Tracefuse now uses its large volume of daily case data to detect drops in success rates that signal Amazon has made a backend change, giving the team early intelligence to adapt.

pending_qa.q: What are the current scale metrics for Tracefuse in terms of brands served and reviews removed?
pending_qa.r: As of the time of the interview, Tracefuse works with 700 brands and has removed over 16,000 reviews. Shane Barker attributes this growth primarily to the last two years of operation, contrasting it with the difficult early period of building the business from scratch.
